title: The NVVSpeech Challenge 2026: Overview and Lessons for Speech Understanding and Generation with Nonverbal Vocalizations

paper.title: The NVVSpeech Challenge 2026: Overview and Lessons for Speech Understanding and Generation with Nonverbal Vocalizations
paper.abstract: Abstract Nonverbal vocalizations (NVVs), such as laughter and sighs, convey meaning alongside words. NVV-aware speech systems must recognize and generate these events while preserving lexical accuracy and perceptual quality. Yet differences in annotation, resources, and evaluation complicate comparisons, and aggregate scores can obscure specific weaknesses. We review ten system descriptions from the NVVSpeech Challenge 2026, covering understanding and generation in Chinese and English across 16 event categories. Our analysis examines supervision construction, task adaptation, and inference-time or preference-based feedback. Results reveal persistent recognition difficulties with breath and gasp and trade-offs between event recognition and lexical accuracy, as well as between generation intelligibility and acoustic quality, with human listening providing complementary evaluation evidence. These findings identify priorities for advancing NVV-aware speech understanding, controllable generation, and comparable evaluation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Natural speech is a temporally organized communicative signal in which lexical content and nonverbal vocalizations (NVVs) jointly convey meaning. Laughter, sighs, breaths, and coughs may express affect, regulate interaction, or reflect physiological states. The central challenge is therefore not only to determine whether an NVV occurs, but also to identify its category, locate it relative to spoken words, and realize it with an appropriate acoustic form. A transcript can be lexically accurate yet omit important vocal behavior, while a synthetic utterance can remain intelligible yet fail to produce, control, or appropriately place a requested event [ 13 , 12 ] . NVV-aware speech technology must consequently address event recognition and generation together with lexical fidelity and perceptual quality. Recent work has advanced this problem through complementary resources and methods. Annotated corpora support NVV-aware modeling in English, Mandarin, and bilingual settings [ 14 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 2 , 11 ] . Scalable annotation and synthetic-data pipelines further reduce the cost of constructing training data [ 14 , 1 ] . At the same time, evaluation has moved beyond aggregate transcription or audio-quality scores: WESR separates lexical errors from event detection and localization errors, whereas NVV-SuperBench evaluates controllability, placement, perceptual salience, and speech quality [ 13 , 3 , 12 ] . These efforts establish the main components of NVV research, but differences in taxonomies, annotation granularity, language coverage, and evaluation protocols still hinder direct comparison. The NVVSpeech Challenge 2026 1 1 1 https://nvvspeech-challenge.github.io/ provides a shared Mandarin–English setting for NVV understanding and generation, with 16 event categories, inline tags, and standardized evaluation protocols. Its open-resource policy enables comparison of diverse training and adaptation strategies, with resource differences considered when interpreting results. We review ten systems, including seven for understanding and three for generation. The findings suggest that more data or class rebalancing alone may not overcome incomplete labels or limited acoustic diversity. Aggregate gains can also mask class-specific errors, lexical degradation, and language gaps, while auxiliary models shape annotation, candidate selection, and preference feedback. Our contributions are therefore to: (1) We present the NVVSpeech Challenge 2026 as a common bilingual platform for comparatively fair evaluation of NVV-aware speech understanding and controllable generation under shared task definitions, test sets, and scoring protocols. (2) We systematically analyze ten systems from the perspectives of supervision construction, model adaptation, and inference or preference-based feedback, revealing how data, model, and feedback designs affect NVV control and speech fidelity. (3) We conduct a retrospective analysis of classwise, language-specific, and within-study results, identifying persistent breath and gasp errors, lexical–perceptual trade-offs, and discrepancies between automatic and human evaluation, and derive priorities for future NVV research. sections.heading: 2.1 Task Definition
sections.text: The NVVSpeech Challenge covers Mandarin Chinese and English with 16 NVV categories: breath , sniff , laugh , cry , cough , throat clearing , sneeze , sigh , gasp , snore , yawn , hum , moan , hiss , lipsmack , and burp . Inline tags such as [laugh] encode event identity and transcript-relative position for two complementary tracks. Track 1: Understanding. Systems transcribe speech into words and NVV tags, preserving event categories, and positions. Each prediction pairs an utterance ID with its tagged transcript. Track 2: Generation. Systems synthesize tagged text, realizing the requested events while preserving intelligibility, naturalness, and acoustic continuity.

sections.heading: 2.2 Data Resources
sections.text: The open-resource setting provides no fixed training set. External data and models are permitted with licensing compliance and disclosure. Meanwhile, outputs must be generated automatically. Public resources. NonVerbalSpeech-38K [ 14 ] provides bilingual media speech, while Emilia-NV [ 8 ] , MNV-17 [ 9 ] , and SMIIP-NV [ 11 ] add word-level, performative, and expressive Mandarin data, respectively. NonverbalTTS [ 2 ] provides aligned English NVVs and emotion labels; SynParaSpeech [ 1 ] adds synthetic speech; and WESR-Bench [ 13 ] annotates discrete and speech-overlapping events. The supplementary Burp_data 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/NVVSpeech-Challenge/Burp_data contains 1,500 synthetic bilingual clips filtered by Gemini without human verification [ 3 ] . Combining these resources requires label harmonization and checks of event identity and placement. Evaluation sets. Track 1 releases 985 Chinese and 961 English recordings, withholding reference transcripts and event annotations 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track1-Test-Set . Track 2 supplies 800 tagged prompts per language 4 4 4 https://huggingface.co/datasets/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track2-Test-Set .

sections.heading: 2.4 Baseline Systems
sections.text: Track 1: Understanding. The Track 1 baseline 5 5 5 https://github.com/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track1-Baseline fully fine-tunes Whisper-medium [ 10 ] , reassigning 16 token IDs to NVV tags without expanding the vocabulary. Training mixes NVV-annotated and conventional ASR speech at a 60/40 ratio; greedy decoding jointly produces words and tags without timestamps. Track 2: Generation. The Track 2 baseline 6 6 6 https://github.com/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track2-Baseline fine-tunes the VoxCPM2 backbone [ 16 ] on paired audio and tagged text while freezing its audio VAE. English-form tags are mapped to Chinese training labels without changing lexical text.

sections.heading: 3 Participating and Related Approaches
sections.text: Table 1 summarizes participating systems and paper-only contributions. Their designs address three distinct bottlenecks: the reliability and coverage of event supervision, the adaptation of pretrained models to tagged speech, and the use of auxiliary feedback. Across these stages, a common design objective is to introduce NVV capabilities while preserving the surrounding speech. The distinctive approaches differ in where they intervene: labels, token distributions, expert routing, or generated candidates.

sections.heading: 3.1 Backbone
sections.text: Understanding systems combine ASR backbones with broader audio-language models. Qwen3-ASR underlies AcoustiX, XingChenAGI, and SighLogger; Whisper-medium supports the baseline and source-adaptive study [ 4 , 6 ] . SMIIP combines MOSS-Audio, Whisper, and Step-Audio, while Audio Team adapts Qwen3-Omni’s MoE decoder. Moss-Transcribe separates the training teacher, Qwen3-Omni, from the deployed MOSS-Transcribe student. Generation uses DiTAR, MOSS-TTS, and VoxCPM2, with VoxCPM2 shared by the baseline and Flow-DPO [ 15 , 5 ] . Backbone choice therefore determines the available adaptation mechanisms: token-level transfer requires compatible token spaces, routing adaptation requires accessible experts, and flow-based generation permits flow-matching preference surrogates. Conversely, the diversity of strategies built on Qwen3-ASR shows that choosing a backbone leaves substantial data and optimization decisions unresolved. The heterogeneous training and inference settings preclude attributing score differences to architecture alone.

sections.heading: 3.2 Supervision and Targeted Coverage
sections.text: SMIIP audits annotations, while the source-adaptive study [ 4 ] filters public data and mines spontaneous NVVs. Co-Refine takes a more structured approach: heterogeneous models trained on disjoint partitions cross-audit weak labels, with teacher adjudication and human review for disagreements. Its distinction is to make label correction an explicit stage rather than treating existing tags as fixed targets. Rebalancing addresses a separate problem: SighLogger adjusts class exposure through square-root sampling [ 6 ] , whereas XingChenAGI uses curriculum learning and clipped resampling. Repetition changes exposure but cannot correct a mislabeled event. Aligned insertion supplies event-position targets; tagged synthesis and voice conversion expand contexts and speakers, as in AcoustiX. For generation, MOSS-TTS screens the requested event region as well as lexical completeness and audio quality. This local focus matters because a fluent utterance may still omit its requested NVV. ASR provides supporting evidence, rather than a complete test of event presence or category correctness. sections.heading: 3.3 Adapting and Preserving Pretrained Structure
sections.text: Moss-Transcribe’s tokenizer-aligned distillation is distinctive: after supervised initialization, the student generates prefixes on official unlabeled audio, and a frozen Qwen3-Omni teacher scores those same prefixes for reverse-KL training. Unlike supervision restricted to reference prefixes, this places feedback on trajectories the student actually visits; the shared tokenizer enables direct token-level comparison. Audio Team intervenes inside the model instead: it disables MoE load balancing and adds Prior Intervention Routing over a frozen gate, aiming to adapt event behavior while retaining pretrained expert specialization. These designs separate transferring output behavior from preserving internal computation; their aggregate scores do not isolate either mechanism’s contribution. DiTAR adds NVV tokens and modifies stop prediction so that internal vocal events are distinguished from utterance endings [ 15 ] . This targets a structural failure mode beyond class imbalance. MOSS-TTS instead emphasizes two-stage fine-tuning on curated mixtures, adapting through supervision and training schedule.

sections.heading: 3.4 Feedback at Inference and During Training
sections.text: Feedback has two roles: revising or selecting current outputs, and changing the model that produces future outputs. For understanding, SMIIP fuses event evidence around a stable transcript, while Co-Refine’s hypothesis-guided correction combines the audio with an initial task-specific prediction. For generation, Tencent-HY selects among five candidates using complementary event, ASR, LALM, and quality signals [ 15 ] . Flow-DPO instead incorporates LALM preferences into VoxCPM2 training [ 5 ] : an utterance-level flow-matching surrogate supplies pairwise supervision, while a chosen-sample SFT anchor retains direct fitting to preferred outputs. The anchor complements relative preference learning with an absolute training target. Candidate selection spends computation at inference; preference optimization moves feedback into model updates. Both require validation of the feedback signals against event control, lexical fidelity, and perceived quality.

sections.heading: 4 Results and Retrospective Analysis
sections.text: Table 1 and Fig. 2 provide complementary views of system performance: aggregate scores, classwise errors, candidate-selection trade-offs, and human listening results. Moss-Transcribe has the highest reported Track 1 bilingual score (66.32) and leads participating Track 2 systems under LALM evaluation (74.8734). Flow-DPO [ 5 ] scores 75.7984 but is a non-participating reference. The following analysis preserves each study’s evaluation scope; cross-system differences do not isolate individual design contributions.

sections.heading: 4.1 Class Weaknesses and Rebalancing
sections.text: Fig. 2 (a) reveals a limitation obscured by aggregate scores: breath and gasp rank among the four weakest classes for both SMIIP and AcoustiX in both languages. AcoustiX’s higher overall score therefore coexists with persistent weaknesses in these events. This recurrence identifies priorities for targeted error analysis, but does not establish whether rarity, annotation ambiguity, acoustic salience, or placement errors are responsible. Rebalancing should consequently be validated rather than prescribed from class frequency alone. In SighLogger’s separate local comparison, square-root sampling scores 66.25, versus 62.33 for natural and 63.51 for uniform sampling [ 6 ] . Moderate rebalancing helps in this setting, but stronger balancing is not uniformly better. Together, these observations motivate distinguishing omissions, category confusions, and placement errors before choosing augmentation or sampling interventions.

sections.heading: 4.2 NVV Control and Speech Fidelity
sections.text: Fig. 2 (b) isolates the effect of candidate selection within Tencent-HY’s fixed five-candidate pool [ 15 ] . DNSMOS-only selection maximizes DNSMOS among the compared rules, but multi-metric selection lowers English WER from 3.480% to 2.132% with lower DNSMOS. Thus, a quality-oriented selector need not choose the most lexically faithful output. This figure supports a trade-off between the plotted metrics; it does not by itself establish which selector best realizes NVV instructions or human preferences. A related tension appears during recognition adaptation: the source-adaptive study increases English event F1 from 0.2964 to 0.5081 while text-only WER rises from 25.58% to 34.98% [ 4 ] . These within-study comparisons motivate explicit checks of lexical fidelity alongside event control and acoustic quality, during both training and output selection.

sections.heading: 4.3 Objective and Subjective Evaluation
sections.text: Automatic evaluation and human listening do not yield identical system rankings. As shown in Table 1 and Fig. 2 (c), Moss-Transcribe achieves the highest LALM score among participating generation systems, whereas Tencent-HY ranks first after human listening scores are incorporated with a 70% weight. This change indicates that the automatic ranking does not fully capture the preferences reflected in the listening evaluation, although it does not establish statistically significant perceptual differences between systems. This discrepancy is particularly relevant when auxiliary models also guide system development. Tencent-HY uses model-based signals for candidate selection, while Flow-DPO uses LALM preferences for training [ 15 , 5 ] . Improvements under automatic assessment should therefore be checked against human judgments, especially when optimization and evaluation rely on similar feedback signals. These findings highlight the need to complement automatic evaluation with human listening tests, since higher automatic scores do not necessarily indicate better perceived speech quality.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: The NVVSpeech Challenge provides a shared Mandarin–English benchmark for event-aware understanding and controllable generation. Our review of ten system descriptions shows that supervision, adaptation, and feedback design shape performance: breath and gasp remain difficult, event-aware gains may reduce lexical accuracy, and candidate selection trades intelligibility against acoustic quality. Human listening offers a complementary perspective on system quality. Future work should improve annotation, preserve lexical and perceptual quality, and report resource and feedback conditions alongside multidimensional evaluation.

Inline tags such as [laugh] encode event identity and transcript-relative position for two complementary tracks. Track 1: Understanding. Systems transcribe speech into words and NVV tags, preserving event categories, and positions. Each prediction pairs an utterance ID with its tagged transcript. Track 2: Generation. Systems synthesize tagged text, realizing the requested events while preserving intelligibility, naturalness, and acoustic continuity. 2.2 Data Resources The open-resource setting provides no fixed training set. External data and models are permitted with licensing compliance and disclosure. Meanwhile, outputs must be generated automatically. Public resources. NonVerbalSpeech-38K [ 14 ] provides bilingual media speech, while Emilia-NV [ 8 ] , MNV-17 [ 9 ] , and SMIIP-NV [ 11 ] add word-level, performative, and expressive Mandarin data, respectively. NonverbalTTS [ 2 ] provides aligned English NVVs and emotion labels; SynParaSpeech [ 1 ] adds synthetic speech; and WESR-Bench [ 13 ] annotates discrete and speech-overlapping events. The supplementary Burp_data 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/NVVSpeech-Challenge/Burp_data contains 1,500 synthetic bilingual clips filtered by Gemini without human verification [ 3 ] . Combining these resources requires label harmonization and checks of event identity and placement. Evaluation sets. Track 1 releases 985 Chinese and 961 English recordings, withholding reference transcripts and event annotations 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track1-Test-Set . Track 2 supplies 800 tagged prompts per language 4 4 4 https://huggingface.co/datasets/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track2-Test-Set . 2.3 Evaluation Metrics For language ℓ \ell , the objective scores of Track 1 and Track 2 are computed as: S 1 ( ℓ ) = 100 [ \displaystyle S_{1}(\ell)=100[ 0.70 ​ F 1 , micro + 0.20 ​ ( 1 − mNTD ) \displaystyle 0.70F_{1,\mathrm{micro}}+0.20(1-\mathrm{mNTD}) (1) + 0.10 ( 1 − min ( Err tagged , 1 ) ) ] , \displaystyle+0.10(1-\min(\mathrm{Err}_{\mathrm{tagged}},1))], S 2 ( ℓ ) = 100 [ \displaystyle S_{2}(\ell)=100[ 0.30 A + 0.25 P + 0.15 N + 0.15 Q + 0.15 E ] . \displaystyle 0.30A+0.25P+0.15N+0.15Q+0.15E]. For each track, the final leaderboard score is the arithmetic mean of the Chinese and English scores. Multi-event normalized tag distance ( mNTD \mathrm{mNTD} ) measures placement error; Err tagged \mathrm{Err}_{\mathrm{tagged}} is Chinese CER or English WER on the tagged transcript, treating each tag as one token. For Track 2: Generation , evaluation follows the framework of NVV-SuperBench [ 12 ] . Normalized components measure event type, count, and position ( A A ), audibility and recognizability ( P P ), naturalness and continuity ( N N ), audio quality ( Q Q ), and contextual expression ( E E ). Missing or nearly inaudible target events receive zero for A A and P P . Both tracks equally average Chinese and English scores. The Track 1 baseline 5 5 5 https://github.com/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track1-Baseline fully fine-tunes Whisper-medium [ 10 ] , reassigning 16 token IDs to NVV tags without expanding the vocabulary. Training mixes NVV-annotated and conventional ASR speech at a 60/40 ratio; greedy decoding jointly produces words and tags without timestamps. Track 2: Generation. The Track 2 baseline 6 6 6 https://github.com/NVVSpeech-Challenge/NVVSpeech-Challenge-Track2-Baseline fine-tunes the VoxCPM2 backbone [ 16 ] on paired audio and tagged text while freezing its audio VAE. English-form tags are mapped to Chinese training labels without changing lexical text. 3 Participating and Related Approaches Table 1 summarizes participating systems and paper-only contributions. Their designs address three distinct bottlenecks: the reliability and coverage of event supervision, the adaptation of pretrained models to tagged speech, and the use of auxiliary feedback. Across these stages, a common design objective is to introduce NVV capabilities while preserving the surrounding speech. The distinctive approaches differ in where they intervene: labels, token distributions, expert routing, or generated candidates. 3.1 Backbone Understanding systems combine ASR backbones with broader audio-language models. Qwen3-ASR underlies AcoustiX, XingChenAGI, and SighLogger; Whisper-medium supports the baseline and source-adaptive study [ 4 , 6 ] . SMIIP combines MOSS-Audio, Whisper, and Step-Audio, while Audio Team adapts Qwen3-Omni’s MoE decoder. Moss-Transcribe separates the training teacher, Qwen3-Omni, from the deployed MOSS-Transcribe student. Generation uses DiTAR, MOSS-TTS, and VoxCPM2, with VoxCPM2 shared by the baseline and Flow-DPO [ 15 , 5 ] . Backbone choice therefore determines the available adaptation mechanisms: token-level transfer requires compatible token spaces, routing adaptation requires accessible experts, and flow-based generation permits flow-matching preference surrogates. Conversely, the diversity of strategies built on Qwen3-ASR shows that choosing a backbone leaves substantial data and optimization decisions unresolved. The heterogeneous training and inference settings preclude attributing score differences to architecture alone. 3.2 Supervision and Targeted Coverage SMIIP audits annotations, while the source-adaptive study [ 4 ] filters public data and mines spontaneous NVVs. Co-Refine takes a more structured approach: heterogeneous models trained on disjoint partitions cross-audit weak labels, with teacher adjudication and human review for disagreements. Its distinction is to make label correction an explicit stage rather than treating existing tags as fixed targets. Rebalancing addresses a separate problem: SighLogger adjusts class exposure through square-root sampling [ 6 ] , whereas XingChenAGI uses curriculum learning and clipped resampling. Repetition changes exposure but cannot correct a mislabeled event. Aligned insertion supplies event-position targets; tagged synthesis and voice conversion expand contexts and speakers, as in AcoustiX. For generation, MOSS-TTS screens the requested event region as well as lexical completeness and audio quality. This local focus matters because a fluent utterance may still omit its requested NVV. ASR provides supporting evidence, rather than a complete test of event presence or category correctness. ZH/EN denote Chinese/English; stars indicate bilingual means. 3.3 Adapting and Preserving Pretrained Structure Moss-Transcribe’s tokenizer-aligned distillation is distinctive: after supervised initialization, the student generates prefixes on official unlabeled audio, and a frozen Qwen3-Omni teacher scores those same prefixes for reverse-KL training. Unlike supervision restricted to reference prefixes, this places feedback on trajectories the student actually visits; the shared tokenizer enables direct token-level comparison. Audio Team intervenes inside the model instead: it disables MoE load balancing and adds Prior Intervention Routing over a frozen gate, aiming to adapt event behavior while retaining pretrained expert specialization. These designs separate transferring output behavior from preserving internal computation; their aggregate scores do not isolate either mechanism’s contribution. DiTAR adds NVV tokens and modifies stop prediction so that internal vocal events are distinguished from utterance endings [ 15 ] . This targets a structural failure mode beyond class imbalance. MOSS-TTS instead emphasizes two-stage fine-tuning on curated mixtures, adapting through supervision and training schedule. 3.4 Feedback at Inference and During Training Feedback has two roles: revising or selecting current outputs, and changing the model that produces future outputs. For understanding, SMIIP fuses event evidence around a stable transcript, while Co-Refine’s hypothesis-guided correction combines the audio with an initial task-specific prediction. For generation, Tencent-HY selects among five candidates using complementary event, ASR, LALM, and quality signals [ 15 ] . Flow-DPO instead incorporates LALM preferences into VoxCPM2 training [ 5 ] : an utterance-level flow-matching surrogate supplies pairwise supervision, while a chosen-sample SFT anchor retains direct fitting to preferred outputs. The anchor complements relative preference learning with an absolute training target. Candidate selection spends computation at inference; preference optimization moves feedback into model updates. Both require validation of the feedback signals against event control, lexical fidelity, and perceived quality. 4 Results and Retrospective Analysis Table 1 and Fig. 2 provide complementary views of system performance: aggregate scores, classwise errors, candidate-selection trade-offs, and human listening results. Moss-Transcribe has the highest reported Track 1 bilingual score (66.32) and leads participating Track 2 systems under LALM evaluation (74.8734). Flow-DPO [ 5 ] scores 75.7984 but is a non-participating reference. The following analysis preserves each study’s evaluation scope; cross-system differences do not isolate individual design contributions. 4.1 Class Weaknesses and Rebalancing Fig. 2 (a) reveals a limitation obscured by aggregate scores: breath and gasp rank among the four weakest classes for both SMIIP and AcoustiX in both languages. AcoustiX’s higher overall score therefore coexists with persistent weaknesses in these events. This recurrence identifies priorities for targeted error analysis, but does not establish whether rarity, annotation ambiguity, acoustic salience, or placement errors are responsible. Rebalancing should consequently be validated rather than prescribed from class frequency alone. In SighLogger’s separate local comparison, square-root sampling scores 66.25, versus 62.33 for natural and 63.51 for uniform sampling [ 6 ] . Moderate rebalancing helps in this setting, but stronger balancing is not uniformly better. Together, these observations motivate distinguishing omissions, category confusions, and placement errors before choosing augmentation or sampling interventions. 4.2 NVV Control and Speech Fidelity Fig. 2 (b) isolates the effect of candidate selection within Tencent-HY’s fixed five-candidate pool [ 15 ] . DNSMOS-only selection maximizes DNSMOS among the compared rules, but multi-metric selection lowers English WER from 3.480% to 2.132% with lower DNSMOS. Thus, a quality-oriented selector need not choose the most lexically faithful output. This figure supports a trade-off between the plotted metrics; it does not by itself establish which selector best realizes NVV instructions or human preferences. A related tension appears during recognition adaptation: the source-adaptive study increases English event F1 from 0.2964 to 0.5081 while text-only WER rises from 25.58% to 34.98% [ 4 ] . These within-study comparisons motivate explicit checks of lexical fidelity alongside event control and acoustic quality, during both training and output selection. 4.3 Objective and Subjective Evaluation Automatic evaluation and human listening do not yield identical system rankings. As shown in Table 1 and Fig. 2 (c), Moss-Transcribe achieves the highest LALM score among participating generation systems, whereas Tencent-HY ranks first after human listening scores are incorporated with a 70% weight. This change indicates that the automatic ranking does not fully capture the preferences reflected in the listening evaluation, although it does not establish statistically significant perceptual differences between systems. This discrepancy is particularly relevant when auxiliary models also guide system development. Tencent-HY uses model-based signals for candidate selection, while Flow-DPO uses LALM preferences for training [ 15 , 5 ] . Improvements under automatic assessment should therefore be checked against human judgments, especially when optimization and evaluation rely on similar feedback signals. These findings highlight the need to complement automatic evaluation with human listening tests, since higher automatic scores do not necessarily indicate better perceived speech quality. 5 Conclusion The NVVSpeech Challenge provides a shared Mandarin–English benchmark for event-aware understanding and controllable generation. Our review of ten system descriptions shows that supervision, adaptation, and feedback design shape performance: breath and gasp remain difficult, event-aware gains may reduce lexical accuracy, and candidate selection trades intelligibility against acoustic quality. Human listening offers a complementary perspective on system quality. Future work should improve annotation, preserve lexical and perceptual quality, and report resource and feedback conditions alongside multidimensional evaluation. References [1] B. Bai, Q. Lu, W.
